World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Small robots drafted to help tackle looming renewable skills shortage
World.content:
In a classroom in Victoria's east, the future of Australia's energy system is being mapped out in black markers.

At Stockdale Road Primary School in Traralgon, students are placing small robots, called Ozobots, onto black lines of maps and coding their every move.

Traralgon is in Victoria's Latrobe Valley, the heart of the state's coal-fired power industry.

The activity is part of a State Electricity Commission-run renewable energy workshop designed to entice kids into potential careers in the industry.

While these kids are at least a decade away from choosing their career paths, the aim is to plant the seed early, in the hope of filling some of the roles in a projected 67,000 workforce.

The Ozobots are programmed to detect and follow a black track on a map. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

According to Jobs and Skills Australia, the transition to net zero will transform at least 38 occupations, particularly in electricity supply, engineering and technical trades.

Jobs and Skills Australia is a body set up by the federal government to advise it and industry about the nation's skills needs.

Its modelling shows a growing risk of shortages in vocational roles, especially electricians and other trades needed for renewable infrastructure.

Alison Reeve says there are short and long-term solutions to consider. (Supplied: Grattan Institute)

Grattan Institute energy and climate change program director Alison Reeve said while programs such as Ozobots would help address renewable energy workforce shortages in the long term, short-term solutions were urgently needed to meet growing demand in the sector.

“Things like the Ozobots are really dealing with the long-term skills problem because that will be making sure that more kids see this as an option,” she said.

But Ms Reeve said the challenge would be building that workforce in time.

"Someone who is thinking about starting TAFE next year, by the time we get to 2040, they're going to be one of the experienced people who's in that sort of cohort of 67,000," she said.

" The question that we've got is what are we going to do between now and 2040? "

The robots can teach students how to apply critical thinking to real-world challenges. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Ms Reeve said short-term workforce shortages could be addressed through skilled migration and retraining or micro-credentialing existing energy sector workers.

"To get to that 67,000, we actually need to make sure that we are attracting people with the right skills into the sector now, but also helping to build up people who've already got some of the skills that could help," Ms Reeve said.

"That's where [you] take someone who's already very experienced, but just give them a small amount of accredited training to allow them to get a particular new skill."

Preparing for the future

For grade six student Brody Appleyard, the Ozobots made a complex topic easier to understand.

"They were really fun, really easy to work out and the codes and things were not too difficult," he said.

Brody Appleyard says the Ozobots were easy and fun. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

" I learnt that renewable energy is the future of electricity. "

Science teacher Megan Burns said the hands-on task helped students engage in a teamwork environment.

"It’s really good to connect kids with real-life science and a hands-on activity in the classroom," she said.

"They’ve been able to show their problem-solving and digital technology skills."

Megan Burns says the activity helped students stay engaged and build teamwork skills. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

SEC student engagement lead Sian Fitzpatrick said the aim was to make complex decisions accessible.

"The Ozobots have little sensors at the bottom of them, they read the black track … the code is a series of colours, blue, green and red, and the order of those colours change the code," she said.

As the robots move across maps, students must consider the environmental and community impacts of specific renewable energy projects.

"Students quite often want to put a wind farm near a camping ground, but when they're encouraged to look more closely, they can see there's koalas in that tree," Ms Fitzpatrick said.

"And that generates a whole conversation about, do we really want to put a project here when we could jeopardise those koalas' natural habitat? And they all choose not to."

Sian Fitzpatrick says the Ozobot workshops are part of preparing young people for the future. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Job shortages risk

The Ozobots reflect a broader push to prepare young students for a changing workforce.

A Jobs and Skills Australia spokesperson said regional areas were expected to see sustained growth in clean energy jobs through to 2050.

"We found that the occupations with the highest growth rates to 2030 were in industries related to electricity supply and demand,” the spokesperson said.

"Our modelling indicated eastern Victoria would consistently grow strongly over the period to 2050."

Stockdale Road Primary School students learn how the renewable energy workforce is projected to grow. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

New clean energy centre

The federal government is working to address the looming skills shortage by investing in education and training.

It recently opened a $50 million Centre of Excellence at TAFE Gippsland in the Latrobe Valley.

The centre's role will be to train workers in renewable technologies, smart grids and electricification.

The Ozobots travel to schools across Victoria as part of interactive workshops, with Gippsland being the most recent visit. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Minister for Skills and Training Andrew Giles said he was aware of skills shortages across the sector.

"When we came into government in 2022, Australia faced the worst skills shortage in 50 years and the second worst across advanced economies," Mr Giles said.

"We've been working day and night to turn that around."

TAFE Gippsland's renewable energy Centre of Excellence opened in April. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

The Latrobe Valley's coal-fired power stations are set to close by 2030, but the region will host a range of solar and wind projects.

TAFE Gippsland apprentice electrician Adam Stevens said that shift was already evident.

"Renewable energy is just part of the future and with investment from our local government into facilities like this, it should reinforce that we are moving forward," the 21-year-old said.

Adam Stevens says investment in renewable energy facilities reflects the growing demand. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Mr Stevens said the use of interactive tools like the Ozobots would help prepare future workers for jobs in renewable energy.

"If you start teaching them now, by the time they reach the age to make good change, they've already got the skills, they've got the information, they've got the infrastructure around them to make that positive change in our environment," Mr Stevens said.

World.title: High Court to hear challenge over murder verdict swapped to manslaughter
World.content:
The case of a Canberra man convicted over the death of his partner will be in the High Court today, after an appeal which swapped the jury's verdict of murder to manslaughter.

Michael O'Connell was originally sentenced to 15 years' jail for murder, but is now serving a ten-year jail sentence after his partner Danielle Jordan died from injuries suffered when she fell from his car as he tried to drive off.

Evidence in the trial revealed O'Connell picked her up from the road and rushed her to hospital, telling staff she had fallen down some stairs.

The trial also heard O'Connell had given various accounts of what happened, including that Ms Jordan fell from the car when it wasn't moving, and said to family members that she had jumped on the back when he wasn't looking.

But there was a 14-year-old witness who maintained Ms Jordan was on the bonnet of O'Connell's car as he drove off.

In the end that was the version accepted even by the ACT Court of Appeal, although there were differences about his state of mind.

Danielle Jordan died of catastrophic head injuries after falling from the bonnet of Michael O'Connell's car. (ABC News: Tahlia Roy)

The Court of Appeal dropped the murder charge finding the elements of the charge couldn't be sustained, but the court reserved its position on whether he should instead be convicted of manslaughter.

Weeks later, in an unusual move, the court decided he should be convicted of manslaughter and the 10-year sentence was imposed.

One of the key issues before the High Court is whether the Court of Appeal had the power to make the substitution.

O'Connell's lawyers will tell the High Court today it did not, especially after acquitting him of murder.

"Whilst it is open to a jury at common law to return a verdict of guilty for a lesser alternative, it does not follow from this that an appellate court has the power to substitute a verdict in the absence of a specific statutory power to do so," O'Connell's lawyers submissions to the High Court said.

" The analysis conducted by the majority … tended to subvert the constitutional role of the jury as the tribunal of fact and ignored the appellate task. "

O'Connell's lawyers will urge the High Court to either allow his appeal and order a new trial confined to the charge of manslaughter, or to consider the second option which questions whether having acquitted O'Connell of murder, the decision to impose the manslaughter verdict was even legally possible.

"Having followed the course of entering a verdict of not guilty to murder, the [Court of Appeal] was bound by s 297 of the Crimes Act and should have determined that neither a re-trial nor a verdict of guilty to manslaughter was available," O'Connell's lawyers' submissions to the High Court said.

O'Connell's lawyers have told the High Court if it accepts that, then the findings against him should be set aside.

Prosecution urges High Court to reinstate murder charge

Separately, the ACT's Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) has lodged a counter appeal, targeting the first Court of Appeal ruling which overturned the jury verdict.

The DPP's submissions to the High Court suggested the Court of Appeal gave its decision on a basis not raised in the trial, or on appeal.

The DPP has also queried if the majority in the Court of Appeal disregarded the jury's advantage in hearing and seeing evidence about the issue of "reckless indifference" in relation to O'Connell's state of mind.

O'Connell's state of mind was critical to the findings.

The prosecution will urge the High Court to throw out the findings of the Court of Appeal in the first instance and reinstate the murder charge.

The South Australian DPP has been allowed to intervene in the case.

World.title: Legal Aid NT flags more cuts to services amid ongoing funding crisis
World.content:
One of two legal bodies responsible for representing vulnerable clients in the Northern Territory is considering making further cuts, six months after slashing its services due to a lack of funds.

A series of leaks to the ABC have revealed the depth of the ongoing funding crisis at Legal Aid NT (LANT), sparking fresh concerns children and adults arrested in Australia's most incarcerated jurisdiction could be left without legal representation.

The leaked documents also show LANT's total funding shrank by more than $3.2 million this financial year, despite the NT government claiming it gave the free service "the financial footing" necessary to continue operating, and spruiking what it described as "the largest baseline funding increase in Legal Aid's history".

Last year, LANT paused all legal aid funding grants for anyone who was not already in custody. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

In November, LANT drastically cut its criminal division to avoid running out of money, including by capping total grant approvals and pausing all grants for anyone not already in custody.

A tranche of letters to legal practitioners, seen by the ABC, has now revealed LANT reached that funding cap within the first fortnight of every month since February.

That means for at least two weeks during each of the past four months, even prisoners in watch houses and jails have been unable to access legal representation through LANT.

This month, the cap was reached within a week.

In a letter sent to LANT director Catherine Voumard last month, Criminal Lawyers Association of the Northern Territory (CLANT) president Beth Wild warned the cuts had delayed the progress of cases through the courts, and resulted in defendants spending more time in custody than they otherwise would have.

But in her response to the letter this week, Ms Voumard flagged the possibility of further cuts.

"Without additional funding being available or a reduction in overall demand and costs, Legal Aid NT sees no present prospect of being able to reverse the reduction of services implemented on 17 November 2025," she wrote.

" Indeed, it may need to consider further reduction of services. "

In her letter to Ms Wild, Ms Voumard highlighted growing demand for legal aid lawyers and an increase in the cost of providing legal services as driving the cuts.

Funding boost hides $3m cut

The NT government, which funds LANT's criminal division, has previously claimed it delivered the service its "largest baseline funding increase" during the 2025-26 financial year.

However, Ms Voumard's letter reveals LANT in fact received $3 million less funding overall compared with the previous year.

Financial year Baseline funding Grant funding Total funding 2025-26 $12.065 million N/A $12.065 million 2024-25 $6.352 million $8.996 million $15.348 million

Law firms will refer clients to another service when they are already acting for a client involved in the same case, a factor the government has said was linked to LANT's service cutback.

NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro last year said LANT's financial pressures were caused by an increase in client load due to referrals from the NT's largest Aboriginal legal service, the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency (NAAJA).

NAAJA has disputed that claim, saying its referrals to LANT have not increased.

In a letter on behalf of CLANT, Beth Wild warned the existing cuts had delayed the progress of cases through the courts. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

The NT government was unable to provide a response by the ABC's deadline, but Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby has previously said LANT was "left in an utter shambles" when the Country Liberal Party came to power.

"We acted immediately to enable essential services to continue with a $3.5 million injection late last year," she said.

World.title: Adelaide University students critical after global data breach
World.content:
Adelaide University says access to the cloud-based learning platform Canvas is back online after a data breach last week, but some students have criticised the institution's communication about the incident.

Adelaide University and Flinders University were among thousands of educational institutions internationally that were left scrambling last week after online hacking group ShinyHunters breached the platform.

The system was taken down for many institutions around the country, preventing students from accessing course information and assessments.

While Adelaide University said access to Canvas had been restored by 5pm yesterday, Flinders University was expecting to be "fully operational" this morning.

Adelaide University students criticised the institution's communication about the incident, which follows difficulties with the university's merger between the University of Adelaide and the University of South Australia.

Adelaide University student Ethan Brown says he learned about the breach through a friend and online articles. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Second-year mechanical engineering student Ethan Brown said it had been difficult to work out what happened until the university advised about the breach.

"It did take me a little while to actually find out [what happened] because I didn't find out directly from the uni, I just heard about it from a friend and from articles online," he said.

He said it was "a little concerning" that the breach occurred so soon after issues created by the university merger.

"It is an unfortunate coincidence for them to happen so close together," he said

" I think for people who have already been affected by the merger, it's a bit of a shock to have so many technical difficulties so quickly in the year. "

Second-year student Shannon Schmidt, who is studying a double degree in international relations and arts, said the incident was "not ideal" and had "messed with a lot of things to do with my course material and submissions".

Major data breach sees student details compromised Education institutions around the country are scrambling to respond to a global data breach that's affected Australian universities, TAFE and state schools in Queensland.

He also questioned why so many universities relied on the same third-party provider, which made them "at risk of such incidents".

"I reckon all unis that have been affected should tighten security, if this wasn't a wake-up call, then I don't know what will be," he said.

His friend, linguistics student Bailey Fry, said many students, who had a test on Friday, were "very stressed" by the impact of the outage.

"We got one email saying there had been a security breach, and then it just kind of went down and no-one really knew what was happening," he said.

"It's just been really poorly managed … and everyone is just kind of figuring out things from the merger, this just kind of adds to it.

"It's really disappointing … we deserve and expect a bit better."

Gemma Vu and Taylor Schwartz say the outage was disruptive. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Similarly, Bachelor of Music Theatre students Gemma Vu and Taylor Schwartz said the Canvas outage had caused "confusion" among students.

"It's been a massive disruption," Ms Schwartz said.

She said students had "worked out ourselves" what had occurred, and they had expected more communication from Adelaide University.

But she said it was "hard to know what more they can do".

"I'm sure they're trying their best," she said.

Almost 9,000 institutions worldwide use the Canvas learning management system developed by Instructure, a company based in Salt Lake City, in the US.

In some cases, users of the platform were greeted with a message demanding a ransom.

Canvas is a digital hub used by schools and universities for submitting assignments, taking exams, checking grades and communication between teachers and students.

Adelaide University was created from a merger between the University of Adelaide and University of South Australia. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Access to Canvas for both staff and students at Adelaide University was suspended on Friday, May 8.

In emails seen by the ABC, the university said it had been advised that "an unauthorised third party had accessed some data associated with Adelaide University's Canvas", and that the institution's cyber security team was "actively monitoring the situation and working with Canvas to determine the exact nature of the data affected".

It also warned staff and students that the data accessed included "some personal information".

"However, there is no indication that passwords, dates of birth, government identifiers or financial information have been compromised" the university said.

Adelaide University did not respond to questions from the ABC, but in a statement posted to its website yesterday afternoon, the university said "temporary adjustments", including assessment extensions, had been put in place "to ensure fairness for all students".

"We understand how disruptive this global cybersecurity incident has been for staff and students, particularly during assessment periods, and we thank our community for their understanding," the statement said.

"The safety of our community has been our number one priority as we have continued to work with Canvas and our Australian Government agencies to reach a resolution."

The university also urged students to "please remain alert to phishing or suspicious communications".

Canvas is a learning management software used by educational facilities across the world. (ABC News)

Flinders University said Canvas access was being restored and expected to be "fully operational" by today after it alerted students to the outage on May 5.

"Our priority throughout this incident has been ensuring our students can continue their learning and are not disadvantaged by the outage," a Flinders University spokesperson said.

"We have taken a careful and measured approach to restoring access, including thorough testing and assurance activities, and will continue to closely monitor Canvas as services return."

Students who were unable to submit work due to the outage were granted extensions.

"Face-to-face teaching has continued across the University, and we are working closely with staff and students as online learning resumes," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Thousands spent on antennas and boosters fails to improve mobile coverage
World.content:
Marten and Sarah Jak say they do not have adequate mobile phone coverage despite living at Waitpinga, which is only about 10 kilometres from Victor Harbor and within 100km of Adelaide in South Australia.

Over the years, they have purchased, installed and manufactured an array of antennas and boosters to improve the mobile phone and internet access at their home.

Waitpinga is a rural area adjacent to Victor Harbor and includes popular surf beaches. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

While Mr Jak accepts that coverage in the country is not as good as it is in metropolitan areas, he is concerned that if his family was at home during a power failure, they would miss emergency alerts of fires.

"Basically, there is no coverage. Zero," Mr Jak said.

"We are in a bit of a valley, and there's a small hill in front of us, but the concern is that if there is an emergency situation, there's nothing really that gives us any mobile phone coverage.

"We can't be contacted or contact anyone in the area."

The Waitpinga area includes the Newland Head Conservation Park, and it is close to Deep Creek National Park, where a major fire burned for days in February.

The February fire in Deep Creek National Park reinforced the Jaks' concerns about poor mobile coverage. (Facebook: Range Hope Forest CFS)

It encompasses the popular surfing areas of Waitpinga and Parsons Beach, which also have poor mobile phone reception available for tourists and visitors.

Mr Jak said it was frustrating when people suggested solutions such as using Starlink to connect phones to wi-fi, because while it was an option, it would cost another $600 for equipment, "plus $120 a month extra" on top of what he was paying now.

"And then if the power goes out, same problem," he said.

" We seem to always be throwing money into a hole. "

Waitpinga Beach is a popular camping and surfing area. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

Mr Jak has contacted Telstra to see if the mobile coverage for the area was due to be upgraded and said he was told it was "on the list".

"I understand it's a problem area," he said.

"Funding is obviously an issue, and they said nothing will probably be done for a couple of years."

Trying to make it work

Over the years, Mr Jak has tried installing antennas on his house but found they did not "give enough gain" to the signal, so he also tried making some himself for different frequencies.

When the 3G network was shut down in October 2024, he found himself trying to make another and said he now had "eight or nine" antennas in the shed from previous iterations.

Marten and Sarah Jak have installed several aerials to boost coverage. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"Every time something changes, I have to make a new one," he said.

He recently tried a booster with a phased-array antenna, which cost about $3,000 and gave what he described as "poor reception".

"But at least we can receive texts ... which is one of the things you need if you have two-factor authentication with things that we need to access at work and things like that," Mr Jak said.

"If we have no reception, we can't even get into our emails, even if we can get internet.

"When we do get reception, it's like, 'Yay, we can authenticate.'

"But it depends on the day, it depends on the weather and, at best, the reception is poor."

He said the only mobile phone tower that provided them with a signal was located at Mount Jagged, more than 20km away.

"Not even the Victor [Harbor] towers give me any signal from here," he said.

Call for mobile black spot funding

Independent member for Mayo Rebekha Sharkie said funding inequities needed to be addressed in the federal budget, including in the area of telecommunications.

Rebekha Sharkie is pushing for mobile black spot funding to be allocated to the area. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

She said places like Waitpinga, Deep Creek and Brukunga in the Adelaide Hills were experiencing "real connectivity gaps", and continued investment in the mobile black spot program to help these areas was needed.

"In regional areas like these, mobile coverage is essential for safety, business and staying connected in daily life," she said.

Telstra says topography plays a part

In a statement, a Telstra spokesperson said mobile coverage was "heavily influenced by the surrounding landscape".

"In areas like Waitpinga, steep hills, valleys and coastal terrain can block or weaken mobile signals as they travel from the nearby base stations [at] Encounter Bay and Parawa," the spokesperson said.

"As a result, rugged topography can create shadowed pockets where coverage is reduced or inconsistent, even when sites are located relatively nearby. We believe this is the issue the customer is experiencing."

The spokesperson suggested the Jaks visit their local Telstra store to see what options might be available to "improve their experience".

World.title: First north-west cloudband of 2026 to bring rain from tropics to Tasmania
World.content:
After the nation's driest April in eight years, an unfavourable monthly outlook and El Niño looming in the near distant future, expectations for drought relief this May were not particularly high.

But in a welcome twist of weather variability, the first north-west cloudband of 2026 will finally develop over Australia this week, delivering a broad band of rain from the tropics to Tasmania.

Elusive rainbands fuelled by tropical moisture

While tropical lows brought abundant rain to Australia's interior in February and March, there has been a notable absence of one particular type of rain-producing weather system this year: the north-west cloudband (NWCB).

NWCBs are the most extensive cloud features observed in our satellite images, stretching for thousands of kilometres from Western Australia to the east coast, and are responsible for up to 90 per cent of cool-season rain across the inland.

According to a CSIRO study, NWCBs are present over Australia on average for 36 days per year, with a pronounced seasonal peak from April to June.

But so far in 2026, a true unbroken NWCB has not been present for even one single day.

(ABC News)

But while NWCBs are behemoths of our meteorology, their presence is somewhat cloaked because they are not depicted on a surface weather chart, such as pressure systems, cold fronts, or troughs.

Instead, they result from an interaction kilometres above the ground between two contrasting air masses.

Specifically, they form when cool, dense air wedges beneath tropical moisture flowing into the mid latitudes, a clash that results in the warmer, humid air lifting and therefore condensing into clouds.

Patchy rain to consolidate from Friday

The first ingredient, tropical moisture, started flowing south over Queensland and the Northern Territory on Monday, leading to patchy rain over the northern interior.

As the moisture travels further south this week, the cloud and rain will spread over the eastern outback, and while the average total will remain below 20 millimetres, the odd storm could help to produce up to 50mm near the Queensland-South Australia border.

This will provide yet another boost to the river flows draining into Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, which already has its deepest water level since 1984.

By Thursday or Friday, patchy falls should reach southern SA, but it is not until Saturday that a true NWCB will stretch across the nation.

This coming weekend will see cold air and warm air in close proximity above Australia, the genesis of a NWCB. (ABC News)

The air mass clash is shown on the map above, with cold air from the west pushing into warmer air over Australia's north and east.

At this stage, rain this weekend is likely to extend from the central and southern NT down to south-east states, although modelling varies on the exact timing, location and intensity of falls.

Loading...

By Monday, rain should have eased across SA, but continue across parts of the Northern Territory, western Queensland and New South Wales, with dry-season falls even possible in Darwin.

All up, the system is modelled to drop from 10 to 30mm across a wide swathe of the country, including most farming regions of SA, western and central Victoria, far west NSW, and south-west Queensland.

It is currently uncertain how much rain will reach drought-affected parts of central NSW.

A healthy dose of rain ranging from 10 to 30mm is ahead during the next seven days across parts of central and south-east Australia. (ABC News)

Follow up falls possible next week

One swallow does not make a season, especially in an El Niño year, but there are signs of more rain towards the end of the month.

And while it is too early to forecast in detail, current modelling is hinting that a new region of moisture might approach Western Australia's north coast next week.

If the moisture can then link with a passing front to the south, the tropical-cool combination could again support another NWCB, but it is really just a lottery at this stage.

So what happened to the dry May and El Niño

The Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) long-range outlook showed the odds were stacked against a wet month.

The map below is the forecast issued in late April, which showed that, for most of Australia, rainfall was likely to be below average.

The BOM's May outlook was indicating a drier month was more likely than a wet month, but thankfully rain is ahead this week. (ABC News)

But here is the thing with long-range forecasts — a 75 per cent chance of below median rain means a 25 per cent chance of above median falls.

And sometimes with the weather, you just get lucky and roll a six, but that does not indicate or change the odds of future outcomes.

Essentially, the surprise soaking this May has no relevance to El Niño's presence or strength this year, and, more specifically, to Australia's weather through winter and spring.

So for now, drier seasons are still likely for the remainder of 2026, and that is to be expected in an El Niño year, but as we have seen this month, nothing in weather is a guarantee.

World.title: Wife murderer issued five year parole period after sexual abuse of child
World.content:
A man who stalked and shot his wife dead on an Adelaide street in 1992 and sexually abused a teenage girl after being released from jail has been handed a five-year parole term in South Australia's Supreme Court.

Court documents state high school teacher Colin Arthur Case murdered his 46-year-old estranged wife Margaret Case by shooting her in a street in the Adelaide suburb of Rose Park on March 23, 1992, after she had left Darwin.

He was sentenced to up to 25 years in jail and was released on parole in 2016.

In October 2024, he was taken into custody and charged with sexually abusing a child he was tutoring in mathematics.

His parole was cancelled in December of that year.

Margaret Case was murdered by Colin Case in 1992. (ABC News)

The girl was 13 years old at the start of the offending.

District Court Judge Anne Barnett sentenced Case to nine years in jail for the sexual abuse, but left it up to the Supreme Court to decide on a non-parole period for the crime.

Last week, Justice Rachael Gray sentenced Case to a five-year non-parole period, backdated to when he was taken into custody.

He will be 91 years old if he survives until his non-parole period ends in 2029.

'Poor insight' into crimes

Justice Gray said Case, 86, had "very poor insight" into the impact of his sexual offending.

She said a report from the SA Parole Board in 2020 noted he also showed no remorse for the murder of his wife, who had left him to return home to Adelaide in 1990.

Case pleaded guilty to both crimes.

Supreme Court Justice Rachael Gray noted the effect Case's sexual offending had on his victim. (ABC News)

Justice Gray said the 86-year-old's health conditions meant there was only a "limited" chance he would live long enough to be released.

"That said, I do consider that it is appropriate to set a new non-parole period to provide some prospect of the applicant being rehabilitated in the community should he reach an age at which he will become eligible for parole, and should the Parole Board at that stage, assess the applicant as being suitable for release into the community," she said in her judgment.

The head sentence for Case's sexual abuse ends on October 15, 2033.

Justice Gray noted the victim impact statement from the child's mother that said she felt guilty for allowing Case to have contact with her daughter.

"The mother of the child notes the victim’s young age at the time that the applicant started sexually abusing her and the inability of her daughter to speak about what he did to her, and the manner in which the applicant's conduct impacted the childhood innocence of her daughter, including the consequences of her daughter having to live with trying to forget the things that the applicant did to her," Justice Gray said.

Colin Case is wheeled into court in Port Augusta after his arrest.

Shot on street outside hospital

Case was arrested in scrubland north of Port Augusta two days after his wife's murder.

Court documents from the time said he used a sawn-off shotgun covered with a blanket to shoot his wife in the back outside of a unit in Rose Park.

She had moved into the unit with a new partner a few days earlier after becoming aware her husband had left Darwin and was looking for her.

Staff from the nearby Queen Victoria Hospital tried to save Ms Case, but she died at the scene.

Ms Case was killed outside a unit near the Queen Victoria Hospital in Rose Park. (ABC News)

Ms Case's murder led to calls for stalking to become a criminal offence, which it did in South Australia in 1994.

Colin Case remarried nine months after being released in 2016.

Court documents showed his new wife became suspicious that her husband was abusing the child he was tutoring, and recorded audio of Case and his victim, which she handed to police.

World.title: 'The sky isn't even my limit': Quadriplegic man invents way to pilot drone hands-free
World.content:
Ever since he was a child, Christopher Hills has dreamt of becoming a pilot.

"I would sit in the schoolyard and imagine flying a small plane, weaving through the various trees," he said.

"It felt nice to picture myself having the ability to have that level of freedom and control over something."

Christopher Hills has used switches in his wheelchair headrest to operate computers for many years. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Mr Hills works as a video editor on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, has cerebral palsy, and is a quadriplegic.

With no use of his arms or legs, the 29-year-old uses switches on his wheelchair headrest to operate computers and help him communicate.

Christopher Hills has adapted existing technologies for his app. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

"It has been really encouraging to see technology develop since I was a child," he said.

"At the age of six, I had access to two buttons, a back button and a forward button in order to turn the pages of an e-book.

" Now, the sky isn't even my limit. Technology helps me play, live and work on the same playing field as everyone else. "

Loading...

How does it work?

Mr Hills has a passion for photography and cinematography and has been working hard to take his skills to a new level.

He has developed an app that uses Apple technology and a Microsoft Xbox adaptive controller to operate a DJI drone to capture images.

An image Christopher Hills took of Mount Coonowrin in Queensland's Glass House Mountains. (Supplied: Christopher Hills)

"As someone with cerebral palsy, traditional drone controllers are completely unusable for me," he said.

"The best I can do with a conventional controller is knock it off a table.

"But with the system I'm developing, I can leverage facial recognition, game controller inputs and accelerometer data on my iPad, mapping it all together to control a drone as if I had two working hands."

Christopher Hills uses head movements to pilot the drone. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Project taking off

Mr Hills is now at the field testing stage for his app, and has already enlisted the help of a quadriplegic farmer in New South Wales who has been using the system to monitor his farm.

A TAFE student with cerebral palsy is also trialling the app to complete her filmmaking course.

Christopher Hills has been working on his drone technology for more than six years. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

"Both are really loving it. They have been instrumental in suggesting features for the app, like the ability to use adaptive gaming joysticks," he said.

"I'm looking for people with disabilities, those who work in the industry and anyone who believes they can make a contribution to making flight more accessible."

Christopher Hills is a passionate advocate for accessible technology for people with disabilities. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Leah Barclay, a senior lecturer in design at the University of the Sunshine Coast, has been working with Mr Hills.

"Christopher is really the visionary on this one, but it's been a real privilege to support this project," Ms Barclay said.

"As someone who teaches students how to fly drones and teaches drone technology in our design program, I've never encountered something quite as innovative.

" The app that Christopher has developed, I think, could be game-changing for many people across the world. "

Leah Barclay says Christopher Hills's determination to create the technology has been "incredibly inspiring". (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

She said Mr Hills's drone flights captured beautiful images.

"I remember the first time Christopher was in one of my classes and he said he wanted to fly like a black cockatoo and be a drone cinematographer, and I remember thinking at the time we'll have a few hurdles to jump through with CASA and drone regulations and compliances," she said.

"But Christopher's managed to be a real pioneer in this space so it's incredibly inspiring.

"He's a better drone pilot than I am."

Christopher Hills has put the call out to other passionate photographers to trial his app. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

The right to fly

Mr Hills is aiming to get his system approved by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) and currently operates under permits.

"When I first approached a drone flight instructor, he told me that I could not complete the course," he said.

A photo of the ocean captured by Christopher Hills. (Supplied: Christopher Hills)

Mr Hills has since obtained a remote pilot licence, and wants to help others do the same.

"My personal goal is to build a career as an aerial photographer and cinematographer, so I can enjoy the feeling of being a pilot and express myself creatively through my drone camera," he said.

"My vision for the future is that everyone gets a fair go in the industry.

"Everyone has the right to learn to fly."

World.title: University board implodes after multiple resignations
World.content:
Exclusive NationalUniversities in crisis University board implodes after multiple resignations Julie Hare May 12, 2026 — 6:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian National University’s 15-member governing body is imploding, with four resignations since chancellor Julie Bishop announced her departure on Thursday. Bishop loyalists Tanya Hosch, Wayne Martin, Padma Raman and Rob Whitfield have all tendered their resignations, according to senior sources who are not authorised to speak on behalf of the university. Then-chancellor Julie Bishop fronts the media after a meeting with ANU staff in September. Alex Ellinghausen That leaves only two of the seven members appointed by Education Minister Jason Clare. They are CSIRO boss Larry Marshall, also a Bishop loyalist, who stepped up to replace former pro chancellor Alison Kitchen who resigned on April 25, and Andrew Metcalfe, a former senior federal bureaucrat, who only joined the council on July 1 last year. The ANU council is made up of 15 members; the chancellor, vice chancellor, seven members appointed by the education minister, and six elected members who represent staff and students. Bishop chaired the nominations committee, which made suggestions for new members to the minister.



One elected member of the council, who did not wish to be identified, said the seven appointed members were loyal to both Bishop and former vice chancellor Genevieve Bell, who resigned last year amid a staff and student rebellion over her restructure program Renew ANU. “The appointed council members never wanted to see Bell go. They backed her in up until the very last minute,” the person said. “They still don’t understand how the ANU community felt last year, and the level of frustration it had with the council and with the VC at the time. Genevieve Bell resigned last year. Alex Ellinghausen “Every attempt to try and communicate to the council, the VC, the chancellor, senior leadership, and executives that there were real issues at hand and something needed to be done, they just refused to see it.” Amid the fallout arising from dysfunction in the upper echelons of the institution, university secretary Phillip Tweedie also resigned last week while sources say general counsel Philip Harrison is on extended sick leave.



Harrison was involved in the university’s response to a series of Signal messages, which were leaked to The Saturday Paper. Related Article Exclusive

ANU Threats of imprisonment, seized phones: The chaos inside ANU The messages between then-provost Rebekah Brown and the university’s deans discussed Bell’s alleged failures in the midst of political, regulatory, and staff and student dissatisfaction with her handling of Renew ANU. In a memo to Bishop, which was uploaded to the council’s online portal, Harrison wrote that Brown’s actions could be interpreted as seeking to advance her own position by replacing Bell as vice chancellor. Brown subsequently did replace Bell and has been interim vice chancellor. However, there has been an outpouring of support for her from students, staff, unions, and local politicians since the memo and emails were first leaked two weeks ago.



Neither Marshall, as the most senior governance figure left at ANU, nor a university spokeswoman would answer questions in relation to movements in the council and senior staff. “In my role at the Australian National University, I’m focused on taking care of the university and its people,” Marshall said. Related Article Universities in crisis The rise and fall of Julie Bishop as chancellor of ANU Bishop said her departure from council eight months before her term was due to end was the result of overreach by the higher education regulator, which took the unprecedented step of preventing her and appointed council members from having input in her successor. “Following unprecedented and coordinated interference, the ANU council is no longer able to charge [sic] its legal and ethical obligations,” Bishop wrote in a statement on Friday morning announcing her resignation. “I fear the collateral from this regulatory overreach will be the next generation of students and staff.”



The council resignations came in the hours after all members were given access to a highly confidential report, which examined allegations against Bishop, Kitchen, and Bell that had been raised during a Senate inquiry last year by people who were either recently or still on council. The university has been in chaos since the massive Renew ANU $250 million cost-cutting program was announced by Bell in October 2024, including forced redundancies and the loss of up to 650 jobs. That plan was abandoned following Bell’s resignation less than two years into her five-year appointment in September. Both the regulator, the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency and the Australian National Audit Office have expressed concerns that the appointed members of council did not fully understand or scrutinise the plan or the financial information provided to them and did not ask if there were alternatives. World.title: ASX set to climb as Wall Street rises; Oil higher
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to climb as Wall Street rises; Oil higher Stan Choe Updated May 12, 2026 — 6:48am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices rose as the war with Iran threatens to drag on for longer, but the US stock market nevertheless advanced to a record close. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent from its prior all-time high set on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 95 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.1 per cent to reach its own all-time high. The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures at 6.32am AEST pointing to a gain of 13 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.49¢. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil climbed 2.9 per cent to settle at $US104.21 after President Donald Trump said the US-Iran ceasefire was on “life support” after he rejected Iran’s latest proposal to end their war. The rejection raises the stakes for Trump’s trip this week to China, where he could urge President Xi Jinping to pressure Iran into making concessions. Xi has influence because China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s sanctioned crude oil. Wall Street recorded another record close. AP The war has already sent the price for a barrel of Brent up from roughly $US70 and delivered a blast of painful inflation through the global economy. That’s because it has shut the Strait of Hormuz and kept oil tankers stuck in the Persian Gulf instead of delivering crude to customers worldwide.



Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Trump heads to China weak and embarrassed Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Still, the US stock market has set a run of records on hopes that the war will not keep oil prices high for very long. Companies are meanwhile producing bigger profits than analysts expected, while signals suggest the US economy is holding up even though households are feeling discouraged by expensive gasoline and tariffs. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 fell, even though the overall index rose. Among them was Mosaic, which reported much weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The fertiliser company is benefiting from higher prices for its products, but it’s also contending with much higher prices for sulfur and other raw materials because of logistics snarls created by the war with Iran. Mosaic’s stock fell 1.8 per cent. Stocks of companies whose customers have the least cushion to absorb higher gasoline prices also struggled, and Dollar General fell 7.6 per cent. Businesses with big fuel bills likewise had sharp losses, including drops of 4.3 per cent for Royal Caribbean and 3.2 per cent for Southwest Airlines.



Helping to offset that was Fox, which climbed 7.6 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. More than four out of every five companies in the S&P 500 that have reported their results for the latest quarter so far have topped profit expectations, and they’re on track to deliver overall growth of nearly 28 per cent, according to FactSet. If that turns out to be the case, it would be the best growth since the end of 2021. It’s not just US companies muscling past analysts’ profit expectations. Globally, companies are on track for their strongest growth in more than four years, according to Deutsche Bank strategists led by Binky Chadha. The boom in artificial-intelligence technology has helped corporate profits rise at a faster rate than overall economies. Outside of earnings reports, Beazer Homes USA soared 34 per cent after Dream Finders Homes offered to buy it in a deal valued at roughly $US704 million. A combination would create the country’s seventh-largest homebuilder, and Dream Finders is asking Beazer’s shareholders to push its management and board to OK the deal after making several attempts itself. Dream Finders rose 5 per cent.



Tech stocks were also strong, continuing their big run amid the AI boom. Gains of 2 per cent for Nvidia and 6.5 per cent for Micron Technology were the strongest forces pushing the S&P 500 upward. All told, the S&P 500 rose 13.91 points to 7,412.84. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 95.31 to 49,704.47, and the Nasdaq composite gained 27.05 to 26,274.13. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The pain of Trump’s war could get even worse Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. France’s CAC 40 fell 0.7 per cent for one of the world’s bigger losses, while South Korea’s Kospi soared 4.3 per cent thanks to gains for Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and other tech stocks benefiting from AI. In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher. The 10-year yield rose to 4.40 per cent from 4.38 per cent late Friday.



Yields had moderated a bit this month, but they remain well above where they were before the war with Iran began. Higher yields can raise rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans going to US households and businesses, which in turn can slow the economy. Higher yields also tend to push downward on prices for stocks and other kinds of investments. A report on Monday said the pace of sales for previously occupied US homes was weaker last month than economists expected. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: How Pauline Hanson and RuPaul helped this Australian composer to success
World.content:
CultureMusicLive music How Pauline Hanson and RuPaul helped this Australian composer to success Linda Morris May 12, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It might have begun as a punchline, but Oliver John Cameron has successfully turned an irreverent university chamber musical about Pauline Hanson into a serious career as a contemporary composer. A decade ago, Cameron was creator of The Colour Orange, an eight-track musical satire based on highlights of Hanson’s political journey. As bill posters cheekily declared: “One Woman. One Nation.” David Rowden and Oliver John Cameron Steven Siewert That show serendipitously led to Adelaide Fringe and more recently Cameron’s selection for a “finishing school” for Australia’s next generation of composers with Omega Ensemble – a contemporary chamber outfit – as an inaugural recipient of Omega’s new Composer Accelerator Residency in partnership with the Bundanon Trust this June. Now, Cameron is developing a chamber piece that will serve as an unlikely fusion of pop and opera with a touch of Eurovision. He hopes to take it overseas.



Related Article Eurovision ‘I do feel the angels’: How Olivia Newton-John has guided Delta to the Eurovision stage “It’s a work about a reality television episode,” Cameron says. “The biggest pop star in the world is retiring, but she must choose her successor through a televised competition. It’s a reality episode played out in opera form.” Seeking a style that is both poly-stylistic and referential, Cameron’s score weaves together unexpected threads, with nods to everything from RuPaul’s Drag Race to Verdi’s Rigoletto. Cameron is observing Omega’s first CoLAB workshop for 2026 at Opera Australia, where this year’s crop of four composers is benefiting from the guidance of Sydney Conservatorium of Music deputy dean Matthew Hindson. The ensemble is workshopping a composition by Beth Roche titled Lambton Worm – an ode to a mythic battle between a villager and a giant dragon – that will premiere in August. Omega Ensemble’s founder and artistic director, David Rowden, says the program is designed to support musicians fresh out of the conservatorium who often find themselves “waiting for the phone to ring”. It’s about future-proofing Australia’s leading composers, ensuring they are given a sustainable path to the global stage. “If only we could do more,” Rowden says, ruefully.



The initiative, now in its sixth year, pairs emerging talent with world-class mentors such as Nico Muhly, Nigel Westlake, Missy Mazzoli and Elena Kats-Chernin. Ensemble Offspring also has a program for emerging composers. Last year, Cameron and fellow composers Alexandra Mison, Cassie To and Callum O’Reilly beat more than 100 applicants for the Omega program, which is designed to be a direct, structured answer to the historic challenge of nurturing new voices. Omega says its program’s success has been so pronounced, and demand so high, that it will expand to Melbourne next year. Behind the scenes of CoLAB Omega Ensemble’s unique “finishing school” for emerging Australian composers (from left): Vatche Jambazian, Neil Thompson, Paul Stender, Mark Ingwersen and David Rowden. Steven Siewert This year’s cohort – Roche, Robert McIntyre, Jessie Leov and Thomas Misson – are each developing a commission for Omega during their nine-month mentorship.



The impact of the program is seen in alumni such as Melbourne-based Alex Turley, who was recently commissioned by the Grand Teton Music Festival. “The opportunities which CoLAB help create are akin to a graduate from a national screenwriting program being plucked by Martin Scorsese to write his next film,” says Omega’s newly appointed chief executive, Michael Napthali. “While we are yet to see that happen in film, the equivalent is happening in music thanks to CoLAB.” Napthali notes that even household names like Beethoven and Brahms once required the support of patrons who believed in the capacity of the “new” to create something important. “For donors who recognise the program’s importance, this is not passive giving. It is participation in creation. The patrons of Beethoven did not know they were underwriting immortality.”



Related Article Updated

Streaming ‘Music kept us going’: Netflix’s new Kylie Minogue series digs deep Arts education is a key objective of federal arts minister Tony Burke’s review into its national arts policy, Revive, with Tuesday’s budget to hint at the resources available for Omega and their like that are not government-funded. Hindson says composers are learning more than just notation; they are learning the psychology of collaboration. “There is a huge difference between sitting in front of a laptop and getting into a rehearsal room,” he says. “While our universities do a great job at training the next generation of composers, the cream of the cream for any composer is in getting your music played by outstanding players such as Omega Ensemble. There’s really nothing better for an emerging composer. It’s where they learn the most. Books and other composers’ scores can only go so far. This is the real world.” As for the inspiration that started it all, the real Pauline Hanson never did see Cameron’s musical. “The conceit of the show was that it took a while for Pauline to arrive, so she was played by all the cast members who eventually all become Pauline,” Cameron says.



While he is tempted to revisit the world of populist politics, his focus remains on his new opera. “I like to write many things at once,” he says. “That way, they all speak to each other.” Omega Ensemble’s NEW NOW showcase is at Sydney’s ACO on the Pier on August 14.
